Home and school support planning sheet

Agree one practical goal, the support adults will provide and a review date. Focus on access, comfort and participation rather than making a child hide harmless differences.

4 min read · Sources checked 26 October 2026 · Editorial information

Go to the worksheet

“Needs to concentrate” is a concern, but it is not yet a support plan. A useful home–school plan identifies a particular situation, explains the barrier and sets out what adults will do differently. It also includes the child’s experience: apparent compliance is not the same as comfort, understanding or participation.

This resource helps families and teachers agree a small, reviewable plan. It is not a formal educational assessment or a statement of legal entitlement. Use it alongside professional recommendations and the school’s own procedures.

What you will take away

  • Choose one situation and one meaningful participation goal.
  • Write the support adults will provide, not only the behaviour expected of the child.
  • Review benefit and distress, including the child’s perspective.

In this guide

  1. Define a situation rather than labelling a child
  2. Choose an adjustment that matches the barrier
  3. Write a goal that is meaningful and achievable
  4. Review and share information proportionately
  5. Printable worksheet
  6. Common questions

01

Define a situation rather than labelling a child

Replace “does not cooperate” with a description: “When the class moves from lunch to writing, J. remains by the lunch area and becomes upset when hurried.” This allows adults to ask whether the difficulty involves transition, understanding, fatigue, sensory load or something else.

Ask the child what would help, using their preferred communication method. If they cannot explain verbally, consider their gestures, choices and consistent responses without pretending those observations prove an internal state. Record a strength or interest too: a support plan should describe the whole learner, not only the problem adults want to remove.

  • Explore why similar behaviours can have different explanations

02

Choose an adjustment that matches the barrier

If spoken instructions are difficult to retain, a visible sequence may help. If the room is overwhelming, a quieter place or an agreed break may be worth discussing. If a transition is unpredictable, advance information and a consistent cue may make it easier. These are examples, not a universal package.

Make the adult responsibility explicit. “Will behave during assembly” gives the child a demand but gives adults no action. “Teacher offers the agreed quieter seating option and checks whether it helps” describes something that can actually be implemented and reviewed.

From a broad concern to a specific support
ConcernPossible adjustment to discussWhat to observe
Loses track of instructionsOne step at a time plus a visible reminderCan the child start with fewer repetitions?
Distress during transitionsPreview the next activity and use an agreed cueDoes the transition require less distress or recovery?
Difficulty asking for a breakAgree a spoken, picture or gesture-based requestCan the child access the break when needed?
Overload in a busy areaDiscuss a quieter option without social exclusionCan the child participate more comfortably?

03

Write a goal that is meaningful and achievable

Choose a goal related to access or participation, such as beginning a task with the agreed support, communicating a need or joining a preferred group activity. Avoid making harmless movement, forced eye contact or appearing indistinguishable from peers the goal.

A goal can be specific without becoming a rigid performance target. For example, the team might observe whether the child uses a break request and can return when ready. If using the request leads to punishment or refusal, the communication system will not be trustworthy. Discuss what adults will do when the child is overwhelmed before that situation happens.

Illustrative shared plan

Situation: moving from play to handwriting. Support: a picture of the next activity, a short warning and a clear first step. Goal: begin with less distress. Review: family and teacher compare brief observations after an agreed period, including whether the child finds the support helpful.

04

Review and share information proportionately

Agree who will communicate, how often and which details are useful. A short factual update may be enough; families and teachers do not need to produce lengthy daily reports. Obtain appropriate consent before sharing medical or assessment information, and avoid circulating sensitive reports in group chats.

At review, ask whether the adjustment was actually available and used before concluding that it failed. Look for benefit, burden and unintended effects. A strategy that increases distress should be reconsidered. If concerns persist, the team can discuss further assessment or professional input. A diagnosis may help explain needs, but families can begin a practical conversation with school while assessment is ongoing.

Editorial information

This guide was developed from supplied teaching notes and the linked sources. Worked examples are fictional illustrations, not patient stories. No named clinician review has been recorded; this is general education rather than an individual assessment or prescription. The original presenters are not represented as authors or endorsers.
